newsitem.title: GERMANY: Reserve shortage send German overnight funds up.
newsitem.headline: Reserve shortage send German overnight funds up.

text.p: German overnight funds ticked higher on Tuesday as banks, facing a sizable shortfall in monthly reserve holdings, scrambled to get accounts in order.
While the morning's range spanned 3.00/10 percent, dealers said the bulk of trades was conducted between 3.05/07 percent, above Monday's 3.00/05 percent range.

Reasons for the rise emerged on Monday as the market realised it was some five billion marks short in its monthly reserve holdings. "We are lacking about 5.5 to six billion marks in reserve holdings that need to be made up before month-end," said a senior dealer at a major German bank.

On Monday the Bundesbank said June's preliminary reserve target stood at 39.8 billion marks. The final reserve target is often some one billion marks higher. Banks, however, held only 39.7 billion marks in non-interest bearing accounts at the Bundesbank on Monday, just 700 million marks above Friday's level. At the same time the monthly average stood at 40 billion marks on Monday, down from Friday's 40.1 billion marks.
"Conditions are a little tighter this morning and the reason for this can be read in the reserve holdings," said a chief dealer at another major German bank.
Realising what they need to do before Monday, dealers hope the Bundesbank will be rather generous at Wednesday's securities repurchase agreement, funnelling fresh funds into the system.

"What will happen with money market rates will largely hinge on what the Bundesbank does on Wednesday," the chief dealer said. Another dealer said: "We expect the Bundesbank will inject at least five billion marks in extra funds into the system to replace the expiring 63 billion mark repo pact." While month-ends have been relatively calm recently, lacking the dramatic jump in rates often seen, June may be different.

As June's month-end falls on a Monday and many companies collate half-year figures at this point, "we could see a slightly more volatile month-end, especially since the annual summer vacation season has begun and there is greater demand for cash in circulation," another trader added.

Looking ahead, dealers however stressed that any gyrations should not be interpreted any change in central bank policies. Instead dealers stick by their beliefs that no policy changes are in the offing. "I don't expect there will be anything new for some time," the senior dealer said.
